items.title: Define the sync contract: change feed, cursors, conflict rules and engine decision
items.outcome: The offline client has a published, versioned sync contract with defined cursor semantics and per-entity conflict rules, and the decision to build or adopt a sync engine is recorded rather than assumed.
items.context: The Android offline queue has no server counterpart. A hosted sync engine appears in the cost model and stack notes but in no epic, and its known pitfall with pooled connections and session variables is unaddressed. Without a contract the client and server will each invent incompatible semantics.
scope: Recorded decision to build or adopt, with cost, exit and tenancy consequences
Change feed shape with monotonic cursors and watermark semantics
Idempotent apply semantics keyed on client-generated identifiers
Per-entity conflict resolution rules including deletes and money-bearing records
Schema evolution rules for a client that has been offline across a change
Explicit statement of which entities never sync because the client can recompute them
Allocation-set conflict rules: a split or budget allocation set converges as a whole set, never per member, so the shares cannot stop summing to the expense
Merge-redirect rules for category and merchant identity, so an entity merged on one device redirects rather than resurrects on another
acceptance_criteria: The contract defines cursor ordering, gaps and restart behaviour unambiguously
Every synced entity has a named conflict rule; there is no default of last write wins for money-bearing records
Replaying a change batch twice is specified to be a no-op and the contract states how the server detects the replay
The contract states how a client that has been offline across a schema change converges
The decision record names the chosen engine approach and the rejected alternative with a reason
The contract states the tenancy requirement that the sync path must satisfy

Allocation-bearing records converge as a whole set: the contract states that concurrent edits to a split or budget allocation set are resolved set-wise, and that a per-member last-write-wins result which breaks the sum constraint is invalid
The contract states the tie-break rule for two concurrent allocation sets and requires the losing set to be preserved for review rather than discarded silently

Category and merchant merges converge by redirect: the contract defines a tombstone-with-redirect shape, states that a client holding the merged-away identifier follows the redirect, and forbids resurrecting the merged-away row
A redirect chain is specified to be resolvable and cycle-free, and the contract states what the server returns when a chain cannot be resolved
No money-bearing or allocation-bearing entity uses last write wins anywhere in the conflict table, checked by a review of the table rather than asserted in prose
contracts_schema: Published in the OpenAPI document with generated Kotlin and TypeScript clients and contract verification
security_privacy: The contract requires tenant scoping on every sync operation and forbids a shared session variable that survives connection reuse
Encrypted fields are specified as opaque to the sync layer
observability: Contract requires the server to expose feed lag and apply failure counts
tests: Contract verification for provider and consumer
Conflict rule tables reviewed against a worked example per entity
Allocation-set convergence table review with a worked concurrent-edit example proving the sum constraint holds
Merge-redirect worked example including a two-hop chain and a rejected cycle
rollout_rollback: Additive publication; consumers pin a contract version and adopt under the expand and contract protocol
non_goals: Implementation, which belongs to the server and client tickets
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo contracts. Owns the specification and the decision record. Server and client implementations follow in their own repositories.

items.title: Implement server sync endpoints with tenancy isolation and pooler safety
items.outcome: The server implements the published sync contract with idempotent apply, deterministic conflict resolution and tenant isolation that holds under pooled connections and concurrent load.
items.context: Offline-first behaviour is already promised by the Android plan, and the known failure mode for this design is a session variable leaking across a pooled connection, which would let one tenant read another's changes. That has to be tested by attempting it, not by asserting it.
scope: Change feed endpoint with cursor and watermark handling
Apply endpoint that is idempotent on the client-generated identifier
Conflict resolution implemented exactly as the contract specifies, per entity
Tenant context established and reset around every pooled connection use
Poison batch handling so one bad change cannot block a device forever
Backpressure and pagination limits
Ledger-affecting apply operations use serializable transactions with bounded retry and jittered backoff on serialization conflict
acceptance_criteria: Applying the same batch twice produces exactly one ledger effect
Concurrent edits from two devices converge to the identical result, proven by a replay test
A sync request cannot observe another tenant's rows under concurrent pooled load, proven by an attack test
A batch containing one invalid change fails only that change and reports it, leaving the rest applied
A client offline across a schema change converges without data loss
Feed lag and apply failures are observable per tenant without exposing content
A forced serialization conflict retries within the published bound, produces one ledger effect and returns an explicit retryable failure after exhaustion
contracts_schema: Implements the published sync contract exactly; any divergence fails contract verification
security_privacy: Tenant context is set and cleared with the connection lifecycle and verified under load
Encrypted columns pass through the sync layer as opaque values
Sync endpoints require the same authentication and step-up rules as the equivalent direct writes
observability: Publishes feed lag, apply rate, conflict rate and poison batch count without record content
Publishes serialization conflict, retry, exhaustion and final-commit counts
tests: Convergence replay test across two simulated devices
Cross-tenant attack test under pooled concurrency
Schema evolution test with a stale client
Forced serialization-conflict concurrency test with exactly-one ledger effect
rollout_rollback: Shipped behind a flag, enabled per cohort; disabling the flag returns clients to direct writes
Rollback keeps already-applied changes valid because apply is idempotent
non_goals: Client behaviour, which is the Android ticket
items.parallel_boundary: Primary repo api. Owns the sync module and its migrations. Coordinates with android only through the published contract version.

items.title: Reconcile the Android sync client against the server contract
items.outcome: The Android offline queue speaks the published sync contract, resolves conflicts as specified, backs off correctly and never silently drops a captured transaction.
items.context: The existing offline persistence ticket assumes a server that did not exist. Reconciling it now, against a published contract, avoids a rewrite later and protects the promise that offline capture never loses a transaction.
scope: Queue reconciliation with the published cursor and apply semantics
Conflict handling that matches the contract per entity and surfaces user-visible conflicts
Exponential backoff, retry limits and poison record isolation
Durable queue that survives process death and device restart
Clear user-facing state for pending, failed and conflicted records
Explicit serialization boundary that carries the random source_event_id and idempotency key but excludes the device-local raw-message digest
acceptance_criteria: A transaction captured offline is never lost, including across process death, restart and application update
Applying the same queued change twice produces one server effect
A conflict is resolved as the contract specifies and, where the user must choose, the choice is presented rather than silently decided
A poison record is isolated after the retry limit and reported, without blocking the rest of the queue
Sync state is visible to the user in plain language
The queue is encrypted at rest with the same protection as the local database
A planted raw_hash or message_digest property cannot be serialized into a sync request, while source_event_id and the persisted idempotency key survive every retry
contracts_schema: Uses the generated client for the published sync contract version; no hand-written request construction
security_privacy: Queued payloads are encrypted at rest and are excluded from device backup
Sync failures are logged without record content
observability: Publishes queue depth, retry counts and conflict counts as privacy-safe local metrics
tests: Instrumented durability test across process death and restart
Raw-message digest exclusion and source-event id retry-stability test
rollout_rollback: Behind the same flag as the server endpoint; disabling returns to direct writes with the queue draining first
Rollback drains the queue before disabling so nothing is stranded
non_goals: Server-side conflict rules, which the contract and server tickets own
